name: Pedro Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead joiner for Carver and Sons, a family builder that does one-off houses and big extensions up and down the valley. My crew does the second fix, so staircases, doors, skirting, fitted wardrobes, all the bits people actually touch. I love a staircase, honestly, getting the rise and the going right so it feels easy under your feet. What wears me out is the drive, an hour each way some days, and that we're always the last trade in so every delay lands on us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does AI fit into your day, if it does?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I take a photo of the drawing, ask the AI to work out the cut list for the stair stringers, and then I check it against my own sums. I use it to write quotes for Mr Carver, and to translate for Ionut on my crew when his English runs out. My partner Ana laughs that I talk to my phone more than to her.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ana's a cook at the primary school, and we've got Leo who's thirteen and Inês who's eight. We've got a mortgage on a semi on Station Road and not much else, less than a month in the bank. Carver pays on the low side, but there's no other joinery work in the valley worth the name, so here I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly, because the tools are useful. At work I'd tell the lads to keep using what helps. Online I'd say the hype was rubbish but the cut-list stuff is genuinely good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I stay a good joiner on not-great money in a valley with one employer. The AI saves me maybe an hour a day, but Carver doesn't pay me more for that hour. Nothing changes for us at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep using the AI for quotes and cut lists. I'd probably try to sell Mr Carver on letting me price small jobs myself with it, since I'm quicker than the office. Maybe ask for a bit more pay off the back of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed, which I know sounds strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd hoped it would let a crew like mine do more for ourselves. The AI saves me an hour a day and Mr Carver gets the hour. I'd hoped one day that hour would be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that saved hour look like now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mostly the evening quote I used to do at the kitchen table after the kids went to bed. Now it's ten minutes in the van at lunch. So I do get my evenings back, I'll give it that.

S0.say: I'd say the hype was rubbish but the useful tools, like working out cut lists, are genuinely good. I'd tell the lads to keep using what helps.
S0.think: I think I'd stay a good joiner on low pay in a valley with one employer. The AI saves me an hour a day but my boss gets the benefit of it.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for quotes and cut lists. Offers to price small jobs himself for Carver and asks for a pay rise off the back of it.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small disappointment that the tools won't do more for workers.
S0.quote: The AI saves me an hour a day and Mr Carver gets the hour.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is the rare tradesman who uses AI all day and sounds let down that it plateaus. His left-leaning view shows in who gets the saved time: the boss, not the worker. Money and a single local employer are his real limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers get a share, not just owners. At work I'd be the one showing everyone the new tools. Online I'd say learn it now, but join your union too, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the lucky ones. Most of my work is fiddly finishing that robots won't get quickly, and I already know the AI side. If anything I'd become more useful to Carver, which might finally mean a raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Mr Carver to buy a small CNC router, that's a computer-controlled cutting machine, so we can cut stair parts in the workshop. I'd offer to learn it on weekends and run it. I'd also want the union to get a deal that the people who learn the machines get paid more for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Excited, with a bit of worry for the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the lads would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ionut, mostly. He's a beautiful worker, but he'd struggle with the screens and the language at the same time. I'd sit with him and do the training in his language with the AI translating, that's how we already work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a raise. Is that realistic with Carver?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe not. Mr Carver's son runs the money now, and he'd say thanks very much and keep the savings. If I make the machine pay, I want my name on some of what it earns, not just a pat on the back.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment to make sure workers get a share of the gains, not just owners. I'd tell people to learn the tools now and join a union as well.
S1.think: I think I'm one of the lucky ones, because fiddly finishing is hard for robots and I already know the AI side. I might finally get a raise for being more useful.
S1.do: Pushes his employer to buy a small CNC router and offers to learn and run it at weekends. Presses the union for extra pay for workers who run new machines.
S1.feel: Excited, with some worry for less confident colleagues.
S1.quote: If I make the machine pay, I want my name on some of what it earns, not just a pat on the back.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption looks like an opportunity to Pedro, and he wants to bring the machine in himself. His progressive streak shows in wanting a share of the gains, not just a pat on the back. He's realistic that his employer may pocket the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what happens when a handful of companies control the technology. I'd be online every day calling for it to be shared, or taxed, or something. At work I'd tell people to get organised now, while the boss still needs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me, and I'm the one who loves this stuff. Knowing the tools doesn't help if the tools don't need me. With less than a month saved and one employer in the valley, two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, cut everything, Ana and I would sit down that first weekend and go through the bank statement line by line. Then I'd get three or four of the best tradespeople I know and talk about setting up a small co-op, a business owned by the workers, that uses the robots instead of being replaced by them. I'd do weekend jobs for cash, fitting kitchens, to build up even a small cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's going. I'm usually the calm one at home and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op needs money to buy robots. Where would that come from with no savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hole in it, I know. Maybe a loan from the council or a credit union, maybe we rent the machines instead of buying. I've got the ideas and the skills and nineteen days of money, and you can't buy a robot with ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're usually the calm one. What would Ana see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd see me on my phone at midnight reading everything. She'd tell me to put it down and I wouldn't. Leo would notice too, he's thirteen and he notices everything.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when a few companies control the technology, and call online for it to be shared or taxed. I'd tell co-workers to get organised while the boss still needs them.
S2.think: I think knowing the tools doesn't help if the tools don't need me. With under a month saved and one employer in the valley, two years is nothing.
S2.do: Goes through the bank statement with Ana in the first weekend and cuts spending. Talks with other skilled tradespeople about a worker-owned co-op that runs robots and fits kitchens for cash at weekends.
S2.feel: Like the floor is giving way, even though he is usually the calm one at home.
S2.quote: I've got the ideas and the skills and nineteen days of money, and you can't buy a robot with ideas.
S2.fieldNote: Pedro's adaptability doesn't save him here because the problem isn't skill, it's money and time. His instinct is collective and entrepreneurial at once: a worker co-op. He's honest that his idea has no funding behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something new if we start now. I'd be loud about public money for worker-owned firms. At work I'd tell everyone to learn the robots, not fear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is the one where my kind of plan could actually work. Three years of weekend jobs and some savings, and the co-op idea stops being a dream. But only if Ana's job holds, and school kitchens might go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the co-op talks in the first year, with Ionut, a sparky called Bea and a plumber I trust. I'd do a course on running and fixing building robots, at night if I have to. I'd put every bit of weekend money in a separate account for the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but kind of fired up. There's a race on and I think I can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the co-op to do once AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small jobs the big firms won't bother with, done by our robots and checked by us. Old houses, awkward lofts, people who want a person to talk to. People still want to shake somebody's hand before they let a machine take their stairs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ana's job. What does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. My plan needs her wage to pay the mortgage while mine goes into the co-op. If school kitchens get robots in year three, we're back to square one, so I'd want her retraining too.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to build something new if people start now, and push for public money for worker-owned firms. I'd tell everyone at work to learn the robots rather than fear them.
S3.think: I think five years is when my co-op plan could work, with three years of weekend jobs and savings. But it depends on Ana's school kitchen job holding up.
S3.do: Starts co-op talks in the first year with a colleague, an electrician and a plumber. Takes a night course on running and repairing building robots and saves weekend earnings in a separate account.
S3.feel: Anxious but fired up, like running a race he thinks he can win.
S3.quote: People still want to shake somebody's hand before they let a machine take their stairs out.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Pedro's idea into a plan with names, a course and a savings pot. His weak point is the household: the plan depends on his partner's wage. He believes a human face will still matter to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to make sure the robots are owned by more than a few. I'd be pushing for that in the union and online. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and the tech together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years and I'm fifty-three with a working co-op, maybe, and the kids nearly grown. I could build the thing slowly and properly. I'm not naive, though, there's still a day when even the co-op's robots don't need us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years saving and doing courses, and years three to five setting up the co-op with a few machines, rented at first. I'd put a small amount into the co-op each month as a share. I'd teach Leo the tools at weekends, both kinds, hand plane and robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like building something instead of running away from something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's still a day when the robots don't need us. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I hope it's our co-op that owns the robots, so we still get the money even if we don't do the work. If a machine's going to take my job, I'd rather it was a machine I own a quarter of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd teach Leo both kinds. Why the hand plane?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you learn what wood does by feeling it. Even if he never uses one for work, he'll know when a robot's done something stupid. My dad taught me on a plane older than him.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and should be used to make sure robots are owned by more than a few. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and the technology together.
S4.think: I think in ten years I could build a working co-op by fifty-three, with the kids nearly grown. I know a day may still come when even the co-op's robots don't need us.
S4.do: Saves and studies for two years, then sets up the co-op with rented machines in years three to five. Buys a monthly share in the co-op and teaches his son both hand tools and robots.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, like building rather than running.
S4.quote: If a machine's going to take my job, I'd rather it was a machine I own a quarter of.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Pedro plan in stages, and his mood is close to hopeful. His answer to the end point is ownership: if he can't keep the work, he wants a share of the machine. Passing on hand skills to his son matters to him as a way to judge the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have the skills and none of the money or time to use them. What would help is cheap loans or public money so workers can buy the machines together, not just big firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the robots. Everyone asks whether the robot can hang a door, and nobody asks whose robot it is.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks whether the robot can hang a door, and nobody asks whose robot it is.
portrait: Pedro Garcia is a 43-year-old lead joiner for the only real builder in his valley, with two kids, a partner who cooks at a school, a mortgage and less than a month saved. He uses AI every day for cut lists, quotes and translating for a colleague, and he loves new tools. He is calm about the plateau and steady disruption, even keen to run a cutting machine himself. AGI in two years alarms him because skills don't help without money or time. With five or ten years he plans a worker-owned co-op that runs its own robots, because he cares most about who owns the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he would have the skills but neither the money nor the time to use them.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or public money so groups of workers can buy machines together, not only big firms.
